name: Load Testing Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing load testing code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing load testing style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing load testing code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing load testing style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When load testing decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
2. Validate load testing outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
3. State assumptions about load testing explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
4. Check that load testing terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
5. Prefer the simplest load testing approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
6. Keep load testing changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
7. Before starting load testing work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
8. Document any non-obvious load testing decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. Re-check edge cases relevant to load testing (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
10. Prefer explicit, readable load testing solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid introducing new load testing abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not silently drop load testing edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated load testing concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting load testing assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about load testing over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
